title: Kingston Council: Using AI in Adult Social Care administration
summary: Kingston reports that Magic Notes cuts documentation time by 50–60%, with supervision write-ups falling from 40 minutes to under 10.
account: Kingston piloted Beam Magic Notes to transcribe and summarize adult-social-care conversations, assessments and supervision. Diginomica reported on 3 June 2026 that the pilot ran for four months from February 2024. The council reports 50–60% less time completing notes and assessments, and supervision write-ups falling from 40 minutes to under 10 minutes. The council's account reports limitations for people with low verbal skills or mental capacity and with poor audio quality. Diginomica reported that Kingston then rolled the tool out across its adult social care teams that summer. On 28 September 2024 The Guardian reported that Kingston was among seven councils using the tool. On 11 February 2026 the Ada Lovelace Institute published a study based on interviews with 39 social workers in 17 councils. The authors found that social workers report time savings from such tools but that the savings are uneven and that errors can enter care records. In June 2026 Diginomica reported that Achieving for Children had adopted the tool and that staff uptake stood at 75% to 80%.
purpose: Reduce social-care documentation work by transcribing and summarizing conversations into usable notes and assessments.
model_version: Enterprise version of ChatGPT run inside Beam's environment

ratings.reason: Reported reductions in case-note, assessment, and supervision writing are task-time savings.
Workers report less documentation effort and time. Improvements in service users’ health or care are unmeasured.

ai_role.statement: Magic Notes transcribes and summarizes care and supervision conversations. Staff review, amend, and supplement outputs. The council attributes documentation savings to this assisted workflow, without establishing improved service-user outcomes.

evidence.citation: Council or project account published in the Local Government Association AI case-study bank. The account provides no independent outcome evaluation.
evidence.title: Kingston Council: Using AI in Adult Social Care administration
evidence.quote: Social workers reported significant time savings in completing case notes and assessments, with an average reduction of 50 to 60 per cent.

evidence.citation: Cath Everett, How two UK councils are using AI note-taking to cut social workers' admin burden, Diginomica, 3 June 2026. The trade outlet has no stake in Beam or Kingston. Its account rests on its own interview with Kingston's interim director of adult social care transformation, who reports that the tool frees time for frontline work; the outlet also describes Kingston as a co-developer of the tool.
evidence.title: How two UK councils are using AI note-taking to cut social workers' admin burden
evidence.quote: Our experience of Notes at Kingston has been a very positive one. We've found it to be accurate and reliable, and it continues to support our team in freeing up time for frontline work.

evidence.citation: Robert Booth, Social workers in England begin using AI system to assist their work, The Guardian, 28 September 2024. The newspaper has no stake in the tool; it confirms that Kingston was using Magic Notes by September 2024 but gives no Kingston outcome figures.
evidence.title: Social workers in England begin using AI system to assist their work
evidence.quote: Councils in Swindon, Barnet and Kingston are among seven now using the AI tool that sits on social workers' phones to record and analyse face-to-face meetings.

evidence.citation: Oliver Bruff and Lara Groves, Scribe and prejudice? Exploring the use of AI transcription tools in social care, Ada Lovelace Institute, 11 February 2026. The independent institute interviewed 39 social workers in 17 English and Scottish councils, along with senior council staff. Many of the social workers used Magic Notes or Copilot. The authors do not name Kingston. They report that time savings vary and that AI errors risk entering care records.
evidence.title: Scribe and prejudice? Exploring the use of AI transcription tools in social care
evidence.quote: while some social workers report efficiency improvements, some find that the additional work required to review AI-generated outputs or processes and workflows specific to their local authority prevents them from saving time with AI transcription tools

must_hold: Practitioners are expected to obtain participants’ consent for recording.
